episodes.158673: An upper-level low moved across east-central Florida from the Atlantic and increased instability. Scattered to numerous storms developed over or just inland from the Atlantic coast and moved west while intensifying. A few of the storms produced strong winds gusts along the coast.

episodes.158708: Daytime heating led to scattered thunderstorms in the afternoon.  Small hail and strong winds were reported.
episodes.158714: Several days of heavy to torrential rains and gusty winds were experienced across eastern Kentucky from July 9th through the 12th. A strong surface low pressure remained parked across Illinois to our WNW, with a frontal boundary expanding eastward and through Kentucky, sinking just south of the state to start the day on the 9th. During the day on the 9th and the 10th, the front began lifting northward through eastern Kentucky as a warm front, becoming the center for convective development, and also allowing for much deeper warm air and moisture advection into the region. As the front slowly continued just north of the state on the 11th and 12th, Kentucky found itself in the warm and unstable sector of the system, with showers and thunderstorms developing, peaking in coverage and intensity during the afternoon hours. ||Given the warm environment, storms were generally low centroid and moisture laden, exhibiting well above normal PWats, in the 2 to 2.5 inch range. Soundings also showed shallow inverted V signatures, indicative of steep low level lapse rates and the ability to easily mix down higher winds aloft. Pulsy scattered convection with heavy rain and high wind gusts were the main concerns. Locations where multiple storms moved over saw high water and some instances of flash flooding. Other locations experienced thunderstorm wind damage as stronger winds transferred to the surface, especially as the storms were beginning the dissipating phase. ||An 850 jet SW to NE, storms that NW to SE oriented were bowing.
episodes.158721: A brief downburst from a strong thunderstorm in Walker County resulted in tree damage.
episodes.158736: Scattered thunderstorms developed in a moderate CAPE, moderate shear environment just south of a warm front that was draped from northwest to southeast across central Pennsylvania during the afternoon of July 11, 2021. Several of the storms produced wind damage, and a few storms exhibited rotation near the warm front.   One slower moving thunderstorm brought urban flash flooding to Harrisburg.
episodes.158737: Thunderstorms formed during the afternoon and evening of the 12th in an environment of moderate CAPE and moderate shear southeast of a stationary front. Thunderstorms initially formed as single cells, then formed into multicell clusters later in the event over the Lower Susquehanna Valley.    Further north slower moving storms brought flooding around Mansfield in Tioga County.
episodes.158845: An area of high pressure remained centered over Nevada, but abundant moisture and moderate instability across New Mexico provided the necessary ingredients for a round of numerous showers and thunderstorms on July 11, 2021. Sufficient deep layer shear also was supportive of organized thunderstorm development and large hail. Thunderstorms initially formed over the high terrain areas with outflow allowing thunderstorms to move onto lower elevations. Several reports of hail were received across eastern New Mexico with a couple thunderstorms producing two inch hail. Meanwhile, flash flooding was once again a concern, especially in south central New Mexico where soils were primed from previous days of heavy rainfall. The most significant flash flooding of the day was reported in Roswell where numderous roadways, yards, and ditches were flooded.
episodes.158893: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to parts of southeastern Pennsylvania on the afternoon of July 12.  Rainfall totals up to 6 to 10 inches occurred in Northeast Philadelphia and in far lower Bucks County prompting the issuance of a Flash Flood Emergency.
episodes.158894: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to parts of southwestern New Jersey on the afternoon of July 12.  Rainfall totals up to 5 to 8 inches occurred in far northwestern Burlington County prompting the issuance of a Flash Flood Emergency.
episodes.158935: In wake of a Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) that moved through the region during the morning hours of July 11th, the air mass remained stable for much of the day, despite a weak surface frontal system becoming stationary across portions of the I-30 corridor of Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas. However, strong insolation throughout the day helped to erode the cloud cover by mid and late afternoon across East Texas, allowing for warming temperatures and air mass recovery. Southwest winds helped to usher increased instability northeast into the area from Central Texas by late afternoon/early evening, with an upper level disturbance rotating east beneath a large upper trough helping to enhance large scale forcing near the stationary surface front and instability axis over East Texas. As a result, showers and thunderstorms containing heavy rainfall continued to develop and move repeatedly over Southern Smith, Northern Cherokee, and Central Rusk Counties during the evening through the early morning hours of July 12th. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6 inches fell across this area, with isolated higher amounts between 6-7 inches falling along the Smith/Cherokee County line near the town of Bullard. These excessive rainfall amounts resulted in flash flooding in Northern Cherokee County, where FM 855 north of Highway 175 near the Cuney community was closed due to flooding. ||While these storms eventually diminished during the mid and late morning hours of the 12th, strong heating and increased instability along the weak stationary boundary again resulted in scattered strong to severe thunderstorms during the mid-afternoon across portions of North and Northeast Texas, with these storms tracking east across Kaufman, Northern Van Zandt, and Southern Rains Counties into Wood County. These storms downed a large tree branch across FM 778 just southeast of Quitman, before quickly weakening shortly thereafter as it moved into Western Upshur County.

episodes.159007: Scattered thunderstorms produced several instances of wind damage across northern Maryland, eastern West Virginia and northwestern Virginia.

episodes.159050: A mesoscale convective system tracking along a warm front moved through much of Pennsylvania during the late afternoon and evening of July 11. With a warm and moist air mass in place, storms maintained organization into the early overnight hours. They finally began to lose intensity heading towards the Pocono region of Pennsylvania due to a loss of surface based instability and a transition to an outflow-dominant storm mode. However, a couple instances of damaging winds were observed as far northeast as the Poconos.
episodes.159051: A warm front was draped across northern Pennsylvania and far northern New Jersey on July 12. South of the front, a very warm and unstable air mass was present. An approaching trough also helped spur the development of a weak wave of low pressure, which tracked along the front during the afternoon and evening hours. This helped add some forcing and shear to an already unstable air mass. The result was scattered to widespread thunderstorm development along and south of the front during the peak heating hours. Some of the storms became severe, with a number of instances of damaging wind across the region. This event was also better known for producing prolific flash flooding near the Delaware River just northeast of Philadelphia, along the Pennsylvania and New Jersey border. Storm coverage gradually decreased in the evening hours as heating and forcing were lost.

episodes.159830: Waves of low pressure tracking along a nearly stationary frontal boundary draped across south-central Illinois triggered numerous thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening of July 11th.  Some of the storms dropped locally heavy rainfall, with as much as 3.77 being reported in Mount Pulaski in southern Logan County.  Due to excessive rainfall rates and already moist soil conditions, flash flooding occurred in a few locations...particularly across portions of Sangamon, Logan, and Vermilion counties.
episodes.159878: With a deep upper-level low centered over the Great Lakes and a stationary frontal boundary draped across the region, several cold air funnels were observed across central Illinois on July 12th.  One of the funnels became a tornado when it touched down in far northwest Champaign County.  Minor damage was observed.
episodes.159933: Heavy rainfall from thunderstorms resulted in widespread street flooding in Madison County.
episodes.159972: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of central Illinois during the afternoon and evening of July 12th.  One storm moved very slowly over eastern La Salle and western Grundy Counties.  Torrential rain produced flash flooding in these areas with numerous roads flooded and at least four bridges damaged.
episodes.160153: A typical summertime pattern prevailed with a few strong thunderstorms producing wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.160232: An upper level low pressure area with very cold temperatures aloft moved towards South FL today through the day. This along with strong daytime heating and high atmospheric moisture led to rounds of strong to severe showers and thunderstorms areawide. Strong wind gusts, flooding, and hazardous marine conditions were the main impacts across the South FL local waters.

episodes.160433: A frontal boundary was draped across Massachusetts. It brought widespread showers with heavy rainfall resulting in localized flooding.
episodes.160470: On July 8th, a cold front dropped south through southern Indiana in a saturated environment. Even with moderate instability and shear values, severe thunderstorms were able to produce wind damage across southern Indiana along the Interstate 65 corridor. In the following days, the front stalled and remained in the area causing isolated wind damage and flash flooding in the same part of Indiana.
episodes.160472: A shortwave moving along the Canadian border interacted with moisture and instability over North-central MT for strong to severe thunderstorm development. Surface based CAPE was generally less than 500 j/kg, but effective shear above 30 kts and DCAPE as high as 2000 j/kg was enough to produce scattered areas of severe wind gusts.
episodes.160745: An unstable environment in Northeastern Pennsylvania allowed for storms, triggered by a passing warm front, to become severe. These storms had damaging winds, knocking down trees and wires.
episodes.160754: A stationary front served as a focus for showers and thunderstorms across North Texas. A few of the showers and thunderstorms resulted in flooding and wind damage.
episodes.160777: A high-based thunderstorm produced very strong wind in and around Big Piney. The strong winds blew down limbs from cottonwood trees and caused damage to two mobile homes in Big Piney.
episodes.160793: A typical summertime pattern prevailed with scattered afternoon thunderstorms across the tri-state region. There were a few reports of wind damage with the strongest storms.
episodes.160801: Flash flooding from thunderstorms resulted in a culvert on Mill Brook near the Connecticut River in Dummerston, VT to be washed away.
episodes.160803: A typical summertime pattern prevailed with scattered afternoon thunderstorms across portions of southwest and south-central Georgia. There were a few reports of wind damage with the strongest storms.  In addition, pockets of flash flooding were observed due to very heavy rainfall of 3 to 5 inches in 1 to 2 hours.
episodes.160806: Heavy rainfall occurred during the late evening hours of the 11th to the early morning hours of the 12th. Two to three inches of rain fell over Schoharie County. The rainfall along with debris blocking a culvert along Gorge Creek resulted in flash flooding in the village of Middleburgh. Several streets were flooded, and work crews had to pump out 15-20 cellars.
episodes.160954: There was an upper ridge centered over southern Nevada and an upper trough over Missouri. A weak cold front moved into West Texas and Southeast New Mexico. Moisture and instability were across the area. Atmospheric lift was enhanced across the higher terrain and along the front. These conditions resulted in thunderstorms that produced hail across the area.
episodes.160987: A weak back door front was pushing into the Rio Grande Valley as a strong upper low moved through the Upper Midwest. Favorable wind shear and instability lead to a couple severe thunderstorms moving into west El Paso which brought hail and wind damage to the area.
episodes.160992: A weak back door front pushed in from the east as a strong upper low moved into the Upper Midwest.  Good shear and instability across southern New Mexico allowed numerous storms to become severe with wind gusts over 80 mph and hail up to golf ball size.  In addition, a nighttime haboob caused a multi-car accident along Interstate 10 east of Lordsburg.
episodes.161227: An active monsoon surge brought several back-to-back days of thunderstorms producing heavy rain, damaging wind gusts, and hail across the state.
episodes.161255: An unstable environment in Central New York allowed for thunderstorms, triggered by a passing warm front, to become severe with torrential rainfall. Rainfall totals of 3 to 4 inches, with locally higher amounts, were reported in 2 to 3 hours. These storms produced areas of high impact flash flooding in many parts of Broome county. Several hundred thousand dollars in damage to public infrastructure occurred, along with an additional major loss to private property in portions of the Towns of Chenango and Binghamton.
episodes.161256: An unstable environment in Northeast Pennsylvania allowed for thunderstorms, triggered by a passing warm front, to become severe with torrential rainfall. These storms produced areas of flash flooding in Bradford county.
episodes.161257: A frontal boundary, coupled with an extremely warm and humid environment, produced another day of slow moving, torrential downpour producing thunderstorms over Central New York. Approximately, 1 to 3 inches of rain fell in a short amount of time. The Southern Tier was again hit with major impacts from flash flooding of local creeks, streams and overwhelmed storm drainage systems.
episodes.161258: A frontal boundary, coupled with an extremely warm and humid environment, produced another day of slow moving, torrential downpour producing thunderstorms over Northeast Pennsylvania. Stripes of 1 to 3 inch rainfall occurred over several parts of the area. The greatest rain totals occurred over a large part of Bradford county where 3 to 5 inches accumulated in just a few ours. The region was again hit with major impacts from flash flooding of local creeks, streams and overwhelmed storm drainage systems.
episodes.161349: Scattered thunderstorms formed across northern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours. Many exhibited weak rotation and some funnel clouds but did not produce severe weather. However, a slow steering flow and persistent outflow boundary across the South Bend/Mishawaka area caused areas of flooding and for a brief window flash flooding as over four inches of rain fell over several hours. Some rescues were needed due to drivers misjudging the amount of water on roadways.
episodes.161362: In the late morning and afternoon hours on July 12th, a fast moving, disorganized cluster of showers and storms along an eastward surging outflow boundary delivered strong to severe wind gusts across portions of southeastern Louisiana.
episodes.161363: A stationary boundary in a warm and humid air mass triggered a thunderstorm that had evidence of rotation via radar signatures across Northeastern New Jersey, mainly Passaic County.
episodes.161364: In the late morning and afternoon hours on July 12th, a fast moving, disorganized cluster of showers and storms along an eastward surging outflow boundary delivered strong to severe wind gusts across marine areas of southeastern Louisiana.
episodes.161389: Monsoon moisture slowly seeped into the region under the big dome of high pressure which was causing record-breaking temperatures, fueling isolated to scattered thunderstorms. As the moisture increased, the main thunderstorm impact transitioned from high winds to flash flooding.
episodes.161459: The combination of abundant tropical moisture, moderate instability and a weak upper level disturbance produced thunderstorms with heavy rainfall across the Concho Valley and Heartland. A few of the thunderstorms produced flash flooding.
episodes.161499: An upper level shortwave brought several rounds of showers and storms. Some of the storms dumped up to 4 inches of rain in a short amount of time causing flash flooding.
episodes.161544: Isolated thunderstorms and storm clusters developed over the North Carolina Piedmont during the evening, producing gusty winds that caused some wind damage in Cabarrus County.
episodes.161678: A few thunderstorms caused localized flooding in San Angelo.
episodes.161703: Scattered gale-force wind gusts occurred in association with thunderstorms enhanced by the presence of a tropical upper tropospheric trough over south Florida and the Florida Keys and strong subtropical high pressure over the western Atlantic.
episodes.161738: A warm and humid air mass remained in place. Diurnal convection produced isolated flash flooding.
episodes.161788: A warm front across the area during the early morning hours gradually sank southward towards evening, providing a focusing mechanism for the development of showers and thunderstorms across northeast New Jersey. These storms developed in a moist environment, with precipitable water values greater than 2 inches, and relatively weak low level flow. In addition, antecedent conditions were quite wet, with 3-5+ inches of rain falling across the area the week before. These conditions combined to result in isolated flash flooding across portions of Passaic County, where a COOP observer in Charlotteburg measured 3.96 inches of rain.
episodes.161817: High pressure weakened over northern Arizona which allowed more moisture to move over the state from the south.  This helped strong thunderstorms to develop over the area.
episodes.161906: Moisture increasing from the south triggered severe thunderstorms across northern Arizona.
episodes.166996: A stationary boundary was situated from west to east across northern OH on July 12th, 2021, and would lift north to Lake Erie by late afternoon. This allowed for a warm, unstable airmass to reside over the region, with surface dewpoints in the low 70s, and PWAT values in the 1.8 to 1.9 range. MLCAPE values were near 1000 j/kg, with slow storm motions in the 20 to 25 kt. range. Deep layer bulk shear was generally less than 30 kts. An initial cluster of thunderstorms developed and moved northeast across eastern Lorain, western Medina, and southern Cuyahoga counties during the morning hours, dropping a swath of 0.50 to 2.00 of rainfall. Additional storms developed in the warm sector late afternoon and moved northeast across the region, dropping an additional 0.50 to 2.25 of rainfall, which caused the flash flooding in areas with repeated rainfall due to storm total rainfall of 1.75 to 4.00.

Widespread significant flooding occurred in Bensalem Township.  There were many road closures including parts of Interstate 95, US Route 13, Woodhaven Road and State Road.  Many individuals were trapped in vehicles by the flood waters, with numerous water rescues becoming necessary.  Flood waters reached houses including some along Allen Avenue, McKinley Avenue and Kings Avenue, where residents needed to be rescued from their homes.  The Lafayette Garden Apartments along US Route 13 at the Poquessing Creek were severely flooded with 80 to 100 units affected.

Widespread significant flooding occurred in Bristol Township.  There were many road closures including parts of US Route 13.  Many individuals were trapped in vehicles by the flood waters, with numerous water rescues becoming necessary including those along Walnut Avenue and along McKinley Street at Wilson Avenue.  Flood waters reached some buildings along US Route 13 in the Croyden section of the township.  Part of Dixon Avenue near Newportville Road was washed out, and residents needed to be evacuated from nearby homes.
